title: Prepositions of Place & Movement
subtitle: Say exactly where something is, and where it is going.
objectives: Say where something is with in front of, behind, next to, between, among, above, below, under, near and far from
Say where something goes with into, out of, onto, off, through, across, over, along and towards
Choose between position and movement: in / into, on / onto
Tell apart the pairs that are easy to confuse: between / among, across / through, under / below

content.intro: At A1 you learned in, on and at. This lesson adds the words that say exactly where something is — and the ones that say where it is going.
content.explanation:
English separates two ideas that many languages express with the same word. A preposition of place answers “Where is it?” and usually follows a verb with no movement in it: be, sit, stand, live, wait. A preposition of movement answers “Where is it going?” and follows a verb of motion: go, walk, run, jump, drive, fly, climb.

Some words come in pairs, one for each idea: the cat is in the box, but it jumped into the box.

rules.heading: a) Place — where something is
rules.body:
• in front of / behind: The cat is sitting in front of the TV. / There’s a garden behind the school.
  • next to (also beside): The pharmacy is next to the bakery.
  • between: I sit between Ana and Leo.
  • among: She found her ring among the leaves.
  • above / below — higher or lower, not touching: A drone is flying above the house. / We live on the floor below yours.
  • under — directly beneath, often covered by it: The keys are under the sofa.
  • near (also close to) / far from: Our hotel is near the beach. / The airport is far from the city.

rules.heading: b) Movement — where something goes
rules.body:
• into / out of — entering and leaving: The dog jumped into the lake. / She took a pen out of her bag.
  • onto / off — to the top of something, and away from it: The cat climbed onto the roof. / He fell off his bike.
  • through — in one side and out the other, with something around you: We drove through the tunnel.
  • across — from one side of a surface to the other: We swam across the lake.
  • over — above something and to the other side: The ball flew over the wall.
  • along — following the length of something: They walked along the river.
  • towards — in the direction of: He ran towards the exit.

rules.heading: c) Position or movement? in / into, on / onto
rules.body:
• in, on say where something is: The milk is in the fridge. / The books are on the shelf.
  • into, onto say where something goes: She walked into the room. / The cat jumped onto the table.
  • The difference can change the meaning: He ran in the park (he was there, running) is not He ran into the park (he entered it).
  • In everyday speech, people often say in and on after verbs like jump, put and fall (“She jumped in the pool”). Into and onto are never wrong there, and they make the movement clear.

rules.heading: d) Pairs that are easy to confuse
rules.body:
• between / among: use between for separate things or people you can name or count, usually two — between the bank and the school, between Ana and Leo. Use among for the middle of a group you are not counting one by one — among the trees, among friends.
  • across / through: across is over a surface, side to side — across the street, the bridge, the river. Through is with something around you — through a tunnel, a forest, a door, a crowd. A park can take both: across the park is from one side to the other; through the park is in among its trees and paths.
  • under / below: under is directly beneath — under the bed, under the bridge. Below is simply lower — the floor below, below zero.
  • along / across: you walk along a river if you follow it, and across it if you go to the other side.

examples: The keys are under the sofa.
I sit between Ana and Leo.
She found her ring among the leaves.
We live on the floor below yours.
The dog jumped into the lake.
She took a pen out of her bag.
We drove through the tunnel and then across the bridge.
They walked along the river towards the old town.
The ball flew over the wall.

commonMistakes.wrong: The bus stop is in front the bank.
commonMistakes.right: The bus stop is in front of the bank.
commonMistakes.why: “In front of” is three words. So are “next to” and “out of”: none of them works without its last word.

commonMistakes.wrong: We live near of the station.
commonMistakes.why: “Near” takes no “of” and no “to.” If you want “to,” say “close to the station.”

commonMistakes.wrong: She took her phone out her bag.
commonMistakes.right: She took her phone out of her bag.
commonMistakes.why: Leaving a container is “out of”: out of the bag, out of the car, out of the room.
A bridge is a surface you cross: across. “Through” needs something around you, like a tunnel.

commonMistakes.wrong: They are sitting into the car.
commonMistakes.right: They are sitting in the car.
commonMistakes.why: “Sit” here has no movement in it, so the position word is “in.” “Into” needs a verb of motion: They got into the car.

commonMistakes.wrong: The lamp is among the two chairs.
commonMistakes.right: The lamp is between the two chairs.
commonMistakes.why: Two separate things, one on each side: between.

exercises.title: Where Is It?
exercises.instructions: Choose the preposition of place that fits the situation.

items.prompt: The cat is hiding ___ the bed. I can only see its tail sticking out.
items.explanation: Directly beneath the bed: under.

items.prompt: In the photo, Ana is standing ___ Leo and Marta — Leo is on her left and Marta is on her right.
items.explanation: One person on each side of her: between.

items.prompt: I can’t see the board. A very tall student is sitting ___ me.
items.explanation: He blocks the view, so he is in front of the speaker.

items.prompt: The parking lot is ___ the supermarket, so you can’t see it from the street.
items.explanation: At the back of the building, hidden from the street: behind.

items.prompt: There is a clock on the wall ___ the door.
items.explanation: Higher than the door, not touching it: above.

items.prompt: We found a small house hidden ___ the trees.
items.explanation: In the middle of a group you don’t count one by one: among.

items.prompt: Our apartment is on the second floor. A family with two kids lives on the first floor, ___ us.
items.explanation: On a lower level: below.

items.prompt: The pharmacy is ___ the bakery — the two doors are side by side.
items.explanation: Side by side: next to.

items.prompt: The hotel is ___ the beach — only a two-minute walk.
items.explanation: A short distance away: near.

items.prompt: The airport is ___ the city center. It takes an hour by car.
items.explanation: A long distance away: far from.

exercises.title: Where Does It Go?
exercises.instructions: Choose the preposition of movement that fits the situation.

items.prompt: The dog jumped ___ the lake and swam to the other side.
items.explanation: From outside to inside the water: into.

items.prompt: She took her keys ___ her bag and opened the door.
items.explanation: From inside to outside: out of.

items.prompt: The cat climbed ___ the roof and sat there all afternoon.
items.explanation: To a position on top of something: onto.

items.prompt: The train goes ___ a long tunnel under the mountain.
items.explanation: In one end and out the other, with the tunnel around it: through.

items.prompt: The ball flew ___ the wall and landed in the neighbor’s yard.
items.explanation: Above the wall and down the other side: over.

items.prompt: We walked ___ the river for an hour, following the water.
items.explanation: Following its length: along.

items.prompt: When the fire alarm rang, everyone walked calmly ___ the exit.
items.explanation: In the direction of the exit: towards.

items.prompt: There is no bridge, so we swam ___ the river to the other side.
items.explanation: From one side to the other: across.

items.prompt: He got ___ the taxi, paid the driver, and walked home.
items.explanation: Leaving a car is getting out of it.

items.prompt: She poured the coffee ___ a cup.
items.explanation: The coffee ends up inside the cup: into.

items.prompt: Which sentence describes movement, not position?
options: The cat is on the sofa.
The cat jumped onto the sofa.
The cat is sleeping on the sofa.
items.explanation: “Jumped onto” says where the cat went. The other two only say where it is.

items.prompt: Which sentence describes position, not movement?
options: The bird flew into the room.
The bird flew out of the room.
The bird is in the room.
items.explanation: “Is in” says where the bird is. “Flew into” and “flew out of” describe movement.

items.prompt: The books are ___ the shelf.
items.explanation: No movement — the books are simply there: on.

items.prompt: She is sitting ___ the car, waiting for us.
items.explanation: “Sit” describes a position here, so the word is in.

items.prompt: Which preposition is the opposite of “into”?
items.explanation: You go into a room and come out of it.

items.prompt: He fell ___ his bike and hurt his knee.
items.explanation: Away from the top of something: off. You are on a bike, not in it.

items.prompt: The children are playing ___ the yard.
items.explanation: They are already there, and they stay there: in.

items.prompt: “He ran into the park.” What does this sentence tell you?
options: He was in the park the whole time.
items.explanation: “Into” means from outside to inside. “He ran in the park” would mean he was already there.

items.prompt: The Atlantic Ocean is ___ Brazil and Africa.
items.explanation: Two separate places, one on each side: between.

items.prompt: After a year abroad, she was happy to be ___ friends again.
items.explanation: In the middle of a group, not counted one by one: among.

items.prompt: We drove ___ the bridge to the other side of the river.
items.explanation: A bridge is a surface you cross: across.

items.prompt: The road goes ___ the forest — there are trees on both sides for ten miles.
items.explanation: With the forest around you: through.

items.prompt: They walked ___ the beach from one end to the other, with the sea on their left.
items.explanation: Following the length of the beach: along.

items.prompt: The helicopter flew ___ the city, and we could see every street from the window.
items.explanation: Above something and moving past it: over.

items.prompt: The temperature is five degrees ___ zero — it’s freezing.
items.explanation: Lower on a scale: below.

items.prompt: He put a blanket ___ the sleeping child.
items.explanation: Covering something: over. “Above” means higher and not touching.

items.prompt: She was walking ___ me, so I stopped and waited for her.
items.explanation: In my direction: towards.

items.prompt: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy ___ here?
items.explanation: “Near here” needs no other word. You would say “next to” and “close to,” but not before “here.”

exercises.title: Match the Preposition to Its Meaning

pairs.right: from the inside to the outside
to a position on top of
in one side and out the other
from one side of a surface to the other
above and to the other side
with one thing on each side
in the middle of a group

items.explanation: Subject + be + preposition of place + noun.
“Out of” stays together, before the place something leaves.
Verb of motion + preposition of movement + noun.
“Next to” stays together, before the noun.
Verb of motion + preposition of movement + noun.
Verb of motion + preposition of movement + noun.

items.incorrect: The bus stop is in front the bank.
answer: The bus stop is in front of the bank.
items.explanation: “In front of” always keeps its “of.”

items.incorrect: We live near of the station.
answer: We live close to the station.
items.explanation: “Near” takes no “of.” “Close to” is the two-word alternative.

items.incorrect: The bank is next the supermarket.
answer: The bank is next to the supermarket.
The bank is beside the supermarket.
items.explanation: “Next to” always keeps its “to.”

items.incorrect: She took her phone out her bag.
answer: She took her phone out of her bag.
items.explanation: Leaving a container is “out of.”
A bridge is a surface you cross: across (or over). “Through” needs something around you.

items.incorrect: He ran towards to the exit.
items.explanation: “Towards” already means “in the direction of”; it takes no “to.”

items.incorrect: The lamp is among the two chairs.
answer: The lamp is between the two chairs.
items.explanation: Two separate things, one on each side: between.

items.incorrect: The cat jumped into the table.
answer: The cat jumped onto the table.
The cat jumped on the table.
items.explanation: A table has a top, not an inside: onto.

items.incorrect: The train went across a long tunnel.
answer: The train went through a long tunnel.
items.explanation: With the tunnel around it, in one end and out the other: through.

items.incorrect: They are sitting into the car.
answer: They are sitting in the car.
items.explanation: No movement, so the position word is “in.”

exercises.title: Maya’s Walk to School
exercises.instructions: Complete the story. Read each sentence to the end before you choose.

items.prompt: Every morning, Maya walks ___ her house and turns left.
items.explanation: She leaves the house: out of.

items.prompt: She walks ___ Park Street, past the bakery, until she reaches the river.
items.explanation: Following the length of the street: along.

items.prompt: She crosses the river by walking ___ the old bridge.
items.explanation: From one side of the bridge to the other: across.

items.prompt: Then she takes the path ___ the small park, with trees on both sides.
items.explanation: With the park around her: through.

items.prompt: Her school is ___ the library and the post office, and her best friend is always waiting ___ it, by the main gate.
items.explanation: Two buildings, one on each side: between. Waiting outside, at the entrance: in front of.

items.prompt: They walk ___ the building together and go up to their classroom, which is right ___ the teachers’ room on the floor below.
items.explanation: They enter the building: into. The teachers’ room is one floor down, so the classroom is above it.

summary: Place answers “Where is it?”: in front of, behind, next to, between, among, above, below, under, near, far from.
Movement answers “Where is it going?”: into, out of, onto, off, through, across, over, along, towards.
In and on give a position; into and onto show movement — He ran in the park / He ran into the park.
Between is for separate things you can name, usually two; among is for the middle of a group.
Across is over a surface; through is with something around you; along follows the length.
In front of, next to and out of never lose their last word.
